prose.def: To be healthy and physically well, and figuratively, to be sound or uncorrupted in teaching, faith, or character.
prose.article: ὑγιαίνω basically means to be in good health, healthy, well—the literal sense behind our word "hygiene." The Majority Standard Bible renders it "sound" in 8 of 12 occurrences (73%), covering both physical health (as in Luke 15:27) and a figurative sense common in the Pastoral Epistles, where Paul speaks of "sound" doctrine, words, faith, and love (1 Timothy 1:10; 2 Timothy 1:13). One striking detail: in the Septuagint it usually stands for the Hebrew שָׁלוֹם (peace/wellbeing, 10 of 12 times), and Moulton-Milligan note it was the standard everyday word for "be well" in private letters, used as a greeting like "I hope you are in good health" or even "good-bye."

issues: The syntactic role data shows 11 of 12 occurrences are vocative, yet the definition is framed as a third-person predicate ('to be healthy'); this morphological reality is not reflected in how the definition presents the word's primary usage pattern.

The article mentions 'Luke 15:27' as a physical health example but the measured senses collapse all 12 occurrences into a single label 'sound,' making no distinction between the literal physical sense (Luke, 3 John) and the figurative/metaphorical sense dominant in the Pastorals (Titus 4×, 1 Tim 2×, 2 Tim 2×)—the definition lists both but the single sense label does not capture the split.

The rare rendering 'good health' (3 John 2) and Abbott-Smith's explicit listing of Luk 5:31, 7:10, 15:27, 3Jo 2 as literal uses versus Pastoral Epistles as metaphorical uses suggests a two-sense structure is warranted, not a single combined label.
The Septuagint background (שָׁלוֹם 10×) is noted in the article but not integrated into the definition, which could enrich the 'wellbeing' nuance beyond mere physical health.

receipts.how: Demonstrates the literal physical sense: the father is told his son has returned 'and your father has killed the fattened calf because he has received him back safe and sound (ὑγιαίνοντα),' showing the word applied to bodily wholeness.

Demonstrates the figurative/metaphorical sense dominant in the Pastorals: 'sound doctrine' (ὑγιαινούσῃ διδασκαλίᾳ), where the word describes teaching that is uncorrupted and doctrinally healthy, not physical bodies.

Shows the word used in a greeting wishing literal good health ('I pray that you may be in good health'), matching Moulton-Milligan's papyri parallels and confirming the physical sense is not confined to Luke.

audit.author_note: Luke uses the word exclusively for literal physical health or wholeness, while the Pastoral Epistles (Titus, 1–2 Timothy) use it almost entirely in a metaphorical sense of doctrinal or moral soundness; a reader of Titus may be misled if only the physical meaning is emphasized.

prose.def: Healthy or sound in body, restored to health; also used of things that are intact or, figuratively, of speech that is wholesome.
prose.article: ὑγιής describes being physically sound and healthy, and most often appears in healing stories—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "well" 4 times (40%) and "healed" twice (20%), while in 4 of its 14 occurrences it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The word ranges beyond bodies: classical and papyri usage apply it to intact objects, and Titus 2:8 uses it figuratively of wholesome speech. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this concrete range vividly—one document describes a rented mill as "safe and uninjured" (ὑγιῆ καὶ ἀσινῆ), another speaks of "whole wine-jars."
prose.caution: The Septuagint Hebrew counterparts listed (such as לָבָן "white" and צָרָ֫עַת "leprosy") don't match the core "healthy/sound" sense, suggesting the digest's LXX pairings may be unreliable.

receipts.how: Jesus asks whether the man wishes to become 'well' (ὑγιής as predicate adjective), confirming the core 'healthy/sound' sense the definition correctly captures
'Healed from your disease' (ὑγιής before ἀπό) shows the word functioning as a predicate adjective meaning restored to health, supporting but also complicating sense label 2's 'made healed' phrasing

audit.author_note: John accounts for 7 of 14 occurrences and uses ὑγιής almost exclusively in healing narratives with sharp theological focus (sabbath controversy, JOH 7:23); the single Pauline occurrence (Tit 2:8) is distinctly figurative, applying the term to sound doctrine rather than physical health.

prose.def: Describing wood that is still wet and full of sap, hence fresh and green rather than dried out.
prose.article: ὑγρός basically means wet or moist, and when applied to wood it describes a living, sap-filled branch that is still green—the opposite of dry. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 23:31, where it is rendered "green" in contrast to dry wood. In the Septuagint it shows up 5 times and translates the Hebrew word לָח ("moist, fresh") four of those times, and everyday Koine papyri use it broadly for wetness, even of "raw" or liquid pitch.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense there rests on a single verse plus outside evidence.
